newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan legislature clears way for organ transplants.
newsitem.headline: Japan legislature clears way for organ transplants.

text.p: The Japanese parliament on Monday cleared the way for Japan's first organ transplant in 30 years with legislation that sidesteps a thorny dispute over the legal definition of death which had frozen the debate for decades.

The revised bill, which is expected to pass both houses of parliament on Tuesday, would allow doctors to remove organs from donors for the first time since 1968, provided the donor gives advance written consent and the family does not object.

Approved by a key committee on Monday, the bill recognises the end of brain functions as legal death, allowing the removal of an organ, only when the donor is tested and confirmed to be brain dead by two or more doctors.
Attempts to alter Japan's traditional view that a cardiac arrest defined death met stiff opposition from religious organisations, conservative politicians and medical malpractice victims' groups.
Proponents have argued that hundreds of heart and liver patients die needlessly each year for lack of access to procedures allowed in every industrialised country outside Japan.

The legislation revises a bill, which cleared the 500-seat Lower House of parliament but then became bogged down in the less powerful upper chamber, that uniformly set brain death as the legal definition of death.

Doctors shied away from performing organ transplants after a landmark 1968 heart transplant at Sapporo Medical College in northern Japan from a brain-dead donor resulted in a 15-month criminal investigation.
Citing lack of evidence, police never filed charges against the performing doctor or the institution.
But the case effectively froze public debate on the issue for nearly three decades, forcing scores of Japanese to seek treatment abroad.

Unable to receive organ donations at home, 33 Japanese have gone abroad to receive heart transplants and 142 have undergone liver transplants overseas, according to the organ recipients group TRIO Japan.
The controversy over the definition of death has made lawmakers loathe to handle the issue.
A similar organ transplant bill was introduced to parliament in 1994, but languished in committee for two years before it died a natural death with the dissolution of parliament last September.

Health experts have said Japan's next organ transplant is still a long way away, because the country lacks an organised system for registering organ donors and even a culture that permits such donations.
Kidney and liver patients' groups say there are far fewer potential donors than patients on waiting lists for the organs, meaning overseas operations would continue to be the rule.
Public opinion has also been divided on the issue, with many people questioning whether politicians should be granted the power to define legal death.

After a series of medical and health administration scandals, including the infection of nearly 400 haemophiliacs with AIDS as a result of professional negligence by drugmakers and government officials, many Japanese have expressed doubts that doctors can be trusted.

Addressing fears that doctors would cut corners on the definition of brain death to facilitate transplants, the legislation calls for imprisonment and fines for physicians who violate documentation rules.
